add_subtopics.title: Exponents, logarithms and percentages
add_subtopics.body:
An exponent says how many times to multiply a number by itself: 2 to the power 3, written 2**3 in Python, is 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. Exponents describe compounding. Growth of 5% a month for a year is 1.05**12, about 1.80, so the total growth is almost 80%, not 12 x 5 = 60%.

A logarithm (log) runs the other way. It answers 'what power gives this number?'. log10(1000) = 3 because 10**3 = 1000, and log2(1024) = 10. The natural log, written ln or np.log, uses the constant e (about 2.718). Logs turn multiplying into adding: log(a x b) = log(a) + log(b).

You meet logs in three places. Log-scale charts give each step on the axis ten times the value of the step before, so a chart can show 10 users and 10 million users together. Log-probabilities: an LLM gives each token a probability, and a sentence's probability is all of them multiplied together, which quickly becomes too small for a computer to store. Adding the logs is safe instead. Log loss, the error that classification models and LLMs are trained to reduce, is minus the log of the probability given to the right answer, so being confident and wrong costs a lot. Perplexity is e to the power of the average negative log-probability per token: roughly how many tokens the model was choosing between.

Finally, percentages. Going from 4% to 5% is a change of 1 percentage point but a 25% relative increase. Say which one you mean, because customers and executives mix them up constantly.
add_subtopics.example: A retail customer's dashboard says conversion 'rose 25%' after an AI search pilot. The finance lead thinks sales jumped by a quarter. In fact conversion went from 4% to 5%: +1 percentage point, or +25% relative. You write both numbers on the slide. Separately, the model vendor reports perplexity 1.67 on the customer's product descriptions, and you can explain it as 'on average the model was about as unsure as choosing between fewer than two words'.
add_subtopics.code:
import math
import numpy as np

# Powers and compounding: 5% growth a month for 12 months
print(round(1.05 ** 12, 3))            # 1.796  (almost 80% growth, not 60%)

# A log answers "what power gives this number?"
print(math.log10(1_000))               # 3.0   because 10**3 = 1000
print(math.log2(1_024))                # 10.0  because 2**10 = 1024
print(round(math.log(math.e), 1))      # 1.0   natural log, base e
print(round(math.log(2) / math.log(1.05), 1))   # 14.2 months to double at 5%/month

# Log-probabilities: multiply many small probabilities -> add their logs
token_probs = np.array([0.9, 0.6, 0.8, 0.3])   # model's probability for each true token
print(round(token_probs.prod(), 4))            # 0.1296 (shrinks toward 0 fast)
logp = np.log(token_probs)
print(round(logp.sum(), 3))                    # -2.043 (same information, safe to add)
print(round(np.exp(logp.sum()), 4))            # 0.1296 back again

# Log loss for one prediction is -log(probability given to the right answer)
for p in [0.9, 0.5, 0.1]:
    print(p, round(-math.log(p), 2))           # 0.11, 0.69, 2.3: confident and wrong hurts most

# Perplexity = exp(average negative log-probability per token)
print(round(math.exp(-logp.mean()), 2))        # 1.67: "as unsure as picking from about 1.7 tokens"

# Percent change versus percentage points
old, new = 0.04, 0.05                          # conversion 4% -> 5%
print(f"{(new - old) * 100:.1f} percentage points")   # 1.0 percentage points
print(f"{(new - old) / old:.0%} relative change")     # 25% relative change

rows: Growth compounds; do not add percentages
Each log-axis step is x10, not +10
log of a probability, always 0 or below
Confident and wrong is punished hard
Not the same as a relative %

replace_subtopics.title: The dot product and similarity
replace_subtopics.body:
The dot product of two vectors of the same length is: multiply each pair of matching positions, then add all the results. For a = [2, 1, 3] and b = [1, 0, 2]: 2x1 + 1x0 + 3x2 = 2 + 0 + 6 = 8.

The dot product is large when both vectors have big numbers in the same positions. It is zero when they have nothing in common, and negative when they point opposite ways.

Longer vectors give bigger dot products just because they are bigger. Cosine similarity fixes this by dividing by both lengths, giving a score from -1 to 1 that only measures direction. Search systems for LLM apps compare a question's embedding with each document's embedding this way and return the documents with the highest scores.

Many embedding APIs return normalised vectors, meaning each vector has been divided by its own length so its length is exactly 1. For unit-length vectors the lengths in the cosine formula are both 1, so the plain dot product already equals the cosine similarity. That is why vector databases offer an 'inner product' (dot product) distance: it is cheaper to compute and gives the same ranking as cosine when your vectors are normalised. Check the embedding provider's docs, or compute np.linalg.norm on one vector; if it prints 1.0, you can use the dot product directly.
replace_subtopics.example: Three help articles have tiny made-up embeddings over the topics [billing, login, shipping]: refunds [0.9, 0.1, 0.2], password reset [0.1, 0.9, 0.0], delivery times [0.1, 0.0, 0.9]. A user asks 'I was charged twice', embedded as [0.8, 0.2, 0.1]. Dot products: refunds 0.72 + 0.02 + 0.02 = 0.76, password 0.08 + 0.18 + 0 = 0.26, delivery 0.08 + 0 + 0.09 = 0.17. Refunds wins. If the embeddings are normalised first, the dot product of query and refunds is 0.99, exactly the cosine score, so a vector database set to inner product would rank the articles the same way.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([2, 1, 3]); b = np.array([1, 0, 2])
print(a @ b)                         # 8   (@ means dot product)

docs = {"refunds":        np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.2]),
        "password reset": np.array([0.1, 0.9, 0.0]),
        "delivery times": np.array([0.1, 0.0, 0.9])}
query = np.array([0.8, 0.2, 0.1])    # 'I was charged twice'

for name, vec in docs.items():
    dot = query @ vec
    cos = dot / (np.linalg.norm(query) * np.linalg.norm(vec))
    print(f"{name:15s} dot={dot:.2f} cosine={cos:.2f}")
# refunds scores highest on both measures

# Normalise: divide a vector by its length so the length becomes 1
def unit(v):
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)

q1, r1 = unit(query), unit(docs["refunds"])
print(round(np.linalg.norm(q1), 6))   # 1.0
print(round(q1 @ r1, 2))              # 0.99  dot of unit vectors = cosine

replace_subtopics.title: Matrices and matrix times vector
replace_subtopics.body:
A matrix is a rectangle of numbers with rows and columns. A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns is called 2 by 3, written 2x3.

To multiply a matrix by a vector, take the dot product of each row with the vector. Each row gives one number, so a 2x3 matrix times a length-3 vector gives a length-2 vector. The vector's length must equal the number of columns, or the multiplication is not defined and numpy raises an error.

This is the main operation inside a neural network. Each layer holds a matrix of learned weights. The input vector goes in, gets multiplied, and a new vector comes out, usually followed by a simple function like 'replace negatives with 0'. Stack many layers and you have a deep network.

The same operation powers search. Put every document embedding in one matrix, one row per document, shape (n_docs, dim). Multiplying that matrix by a query vector gives one similarity score per document in a single step, much faster than a Python loop. np.argsort(-scores)[:k] then returns the positions of the k highest scores (the minus sign sorts from highest to lowest).

The transpose, written .T, swaps rows and columns, so shape (4, 3) becomes (3, 4). You need it when you score a batch of queries at once: queries (2, 3) @ docs.T (3, 4) gives a (2, 4) table of every query against every document. The rule for A @ B is that A's number of columns must equal B's number of rows. Most 'shapes not aligned' or 'mismatch in its core dimension' errors mean a missing .T or a vector that should have been a batch; print .shape on both sides first.
replace_subtopics.example: W = [[1, 0, 1], [0, 2, 0]] and a = [2, 1, 3]. Row one: 1x2 + 0x1 + 1x3 = 5. Row two: 0x2 + 2x1 + 0x3 = 2. So W times a = [5, 2]. In business terms: if the rows are two shops' price lists and a is a shopping basket, the result is the basket's total at each shop. For search, four help articles become a (4, 3) matrix D. D @ query gives [0.76, 0.26, 0.17, 0.59], and the top two are refunds and invoices.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

W = np.array([[1, 0, 1],       # 2 rows, 3 columns: shape (2, 3)
              [0, 2, 0]])
a = np.array([2, 1, 3])        # length 3, matches 3 columns

print(W.shape)                 # (2, 3)
print(W @ a)                   # [5 2]  one dot product per row

# A tiny neural network layer: weights, then 'negatives become 0'
W1 = np.array([[0.5, -1.0, 0.2],
               [1.0,  0.3, -0.4]])
h = np.maximum(0, W1 @ a)      # ReLU function
print(h)                       # [0.6 1.1]

# W @ np.array([1, 2])  would fail: shapes (2,3) and (2,) do not match

# Score every document at once: one row per document embedding
names = ["refunds", "password reset", "delivery times", "invoices"]
D = np.array([[0.9, 0.1, 0.2],
              [0.1, 0.9, 0.0],
              [0.1, 0.0, 0.9],
              [0.7, 0.0, 0.3]])            # shape (4, 3): 4 docs, dimension 3
query = np.array([0.8, 0.2, 0.1])          # shape (3,)

scores = D @ query                         # shape (4,): one score per doc
print(scores.round(2))                     # [0.76 0.26 0.17 0.59]
top_k = np.argsort(-scores)[:2]            # indexes of the 2 highest scores
print([names[i] for i in top_k])           # ['refunds', 'invoices']

# Transpose swaps rows and columns: (4, 3) becomes (3, 4)
print(D.T.shape)                           # (3, 4)
Q = np.array([[0.8, 0.2, 0.1],
              [0.1, 0.8, 0.1]])            # 2 queries in a batch: shape (2, 3)
print((Q @ D.T).shape)                     # (2, 4): each query against each doc
# Q @ D  fails: (2, 3) @ (4, 3), the inner sizes 3 and 4 do not match

replace_subtopics.title: Probability and softmax
replace_subtopics.body:
A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is: 0 means never, 1 means certain, 0.5 means half the time. If you list every possible outcome, their probabilities add up to exactly 1.

A model's last layer outputs raw scores, one per possible answer. These are also called logits and can be any size, including negative. Softmax converts them into probabilities in two steps: raise e (a constant, about 2.718) to the power of each score, which makes every value positive and exaggerates differences, then divide each by the total.

An LLM does this over its whole vocabulary, often tens of thousands of tokens, to get the probability of each possible next token. A setting called temperature divides the scores before softmax: a low temperature makes the top choice dominate, a high temperature spreads the probability out, which gives more varied text.

A conditional probability is the chance of one thing given that another is true, written P(A | B) and read 'probability of A given B'. It is easy to confuse P(flagged | fraud) with P(fraud | flagged), and the gap between them is driven by the base rate: how common the thing is in the first place. When the thing you look for is rare, even an accurate detector produces mostly false alarms, because the few real cases are swamped by small error rates on the huge number of normal cases. Always ask for the base rate before you judge a model's accuracy claim.
replace_subtopics.example: A support ticket classifier gives raw scores billing 2.0, technical 1.0, other 0.1. e^2.0 is about 7.39, e^1.0 about 2.72, e^0.1 about 1.11. The total is about 11.21. Dividing gives billing 0.66, technical 0.24, other 0.10. They add to 1, and billing is the most likely category. Base rates: a bank's fraud flag catches 99% of fraud and wrongly flags only 1% of normal payments. Fraud is 0.1% of payments. Out of 100,000 payments, 100 are fraud and 99 of those are flagged, but 1% of the 99,900 normal ones, 999 payments, are flagged too. Only 99 of the 1,098 flagged payments are fraud, about 9%. The analysts reviewing flags will see roughly ten false alarms for every real case, so plan the review queue with that in mind.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

def softmax(scores, temperature=1.0):
    z = np.array(scores) / temperature
    z = z - z.max()                  # avoids overflow, same result
    e = np.exp(z)                    # e to the power of each score
    return e / e.sum()               # divide by the total

scores = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]             # billing, technical, other
print(softmax(scores).round(2))      # [0.66 0.24 0.1 ]
print(softmax(scores).sum())         # 1.0 (up to rounding)

print(softmax(scores, 0.5).round(2)) # low temp: top choice dominates
print(softmax(scores, 2.0).round(2)) # high temp: more spread out

# Base rates: a "99% accurate" fraud flag on 100,000 transactions
cases = 100_000
fraud = int(cases * 0.001)           # base rate 0.1% -> 100 real frauds
legit = cases - fraud                # 99,900 normal transactions
caught = fraud * 0.99                # flags 99% of fraud: 99
false_alarms = legit * 0.01          # wrongly flags 1% of normal ones: 999
flagged = caught + false_alarms
print(f"flagged {flagged:.0f}, of which fraud {caught:.0f}")        # flagged 1098, of which fraud 99
print(f"P(fraud | flagged) = {caught / flagged:.1%}")                # 9.0%

add_glossary: Exponent
The power a number is raised to; 2**3 means 2 x 2 x 2.
Logarithm
The power you must raise a base to in order to get a number; log10(1000) = 3.
Log-probability
The log of a probability; models add these instead of multiplying tiny probabilities.
Perplexity
e to the power of the average negative log-probability per token; lower means the model is less surprised.
Percentage point
The plain difference between two percentages, such as 4% to 5% being 1 point.
Normalised vector
A vector divided by its own length so its length is 1.
Transpose
Swapping a matrix's rows and columns, written .T in numpy.
Base rate
How common something is before any test or model is applied.
Conditional probability
The probability of A given that B is true, written P(A | B).

add_subtopics.title: Installing software and running your own service
add_subtopics.body:
Before installing anything on a customer server, find out what it is. cat /etc/os-release names the distribution and version, for example Ubuntu 24.04 or Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9. uname -m shows the CPU type: x86_64 or aarch64 (ARM). Both decide which packages and Docker images will work.

Software comes from the distribution's package manager. Debian and Ubuntu use apt (sudo apt update, then sudo apt install python3-venv). Red Hat, Rocky and Amazon Linux use dnf (sudo dnf install python3.12). Many customers only allow approved packages, so ask before installing and write down what you added.

To keep your app running after you log out, and to restart it after a crash or reboot, write a systemd unit file in /etc/systemd/system/, such as qa-service.service. The important lines are: User= (run as a dedicated, unprivileged user, never root), WorkingDirectory= (the app folder), EnvironmentFile= (a file of KEY=value settings, mode 600), ExecStart= (the full command, with absolute paths), and Restart=on-failure with RestartSec=5.

After creating or editing a unit, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd reads it, then sudo systemctl enable --now qa-service to start it now and at every boot. Check it with systemctl status and journalctl -u qa-service.

If your app writes its own log file instead of the journal, add a logrotate rule in /etc/logrotate.d/ so old logs are compressed and deleted. That prevents the full-disk outage from the first subtopic.
add_subtopics.example: An FDE deploys a Q&A service on a logistics customer's Ubuntu 24.04 VM. cat /etc/os-release and uname -m confirm Ubuntu on x86_64. She installs python3-venv with apt, creates a qa user, puts the code in /opt/qa-service and the API key in /etc/qa-service/env with mode 600. The unit file below starts uvicorn as qa. After a reboot test during the change window, systemctl status shows the service active again within seconds, and a forced crash shows systemd restarting it after 5 seconds.
add_subtopics.code:
cat /etc/os-release | head -3      # which distribution and version?
uname -m                           # x86_64 or aarch64

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3-venv   # Debian/Ubuntu
# sudo dnf install -y python3.12                      # RHEL/Rocky/Amazon Linux

sudo useradd --system --home /opt/qa-service --shell /usr/sbin/nologin qa

# /etc/systemd/system/qa-service.service
# [Unit]
# Description=Q&A service
# After=network-online.target
# Wants=network-online.target
#
# [Service]
# User=qa
# WorkingDirectory=/opt/qa-service
# EnvironmentFile=/etc/qa-service/env          # KEY=value lines, chmod 600
# ExecStart=/opt/qa-service/.venv/bin/uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
# Restart=on-failure
# RestartSec=5
#
# [Install]
# WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload               # read new or changed unit files
sudo systemctl enable --now qa-service     # start now and at every boot
systemctl status qa-service                # active (running)?
journalctl -u qa-service -n 50             # last 50 log lines

# /etc/logrotate.d/qa-service  (only if the app writes its own log files)
# /var/log/qa/*.log {
#     daily
#     rotate 14
#     compress
#     missingok
#     notifempty
#     copytruncate
# }
checklist: Checked the OS and CPU type (os-release, uname -m)
Asked before installing packages and recorded what was added
Service runs as its own non-root user
Secrets in an EnvironmentFile with mode 600
Absolute paths in ExecStart
Restart=on-failure set
daemon-reload, then enable --now
Reboot tested and logs rotated

replace_subtopics.title: The filesystem and moving around
replace_subtopics.body:
Linux has one tree of folders (called directories) starting at the root, written /. There are no drive letters. A path like /var/log/nginx/error.log reads from the root down. A path that does not start with / is relative to where you are now, which pwd (print working directory) shows.

A few directories matter every day. /etc holds configuration files. /var/log holds logs. /home/yourname is your home directory, shortened to ~. /tmp is scratch space that may be wiped. /opt and /srv often hold installed applications.

The basic commands are ls to list, cd to move, cat to print a file, less to page through one, cp and mv to copy and move, rm to delete, mkdir to make a directory, and find to search by name. df -h shows free disk space and du -sh shows how big a folder is. A full disk is one of the most common reasons a service suddenly stops.

On a server there is no mouse, so you edit files in a terminal editor. nano is the friendly one: type to edit, Ctrl+O then Enter to save, Ctrl+X to exit (the shortcuts are listed at the bottom of the screen). Many servers only have vim, which opens in a mode where keys are commands, not text. Press i to start typing, Esc to stop, then type :wq and Enter to save and quit, or :q! and Enter to quit without saving. Knowing how to leave vim saves a lot of panic.

To empty a huge log without deleting it, truncate it: truncate -s 0 file or : > file sets its size to zero while the program keeps writing to the same file. Deleting it with rm is a trap if a process still has the file open: the name disappears, but the disk space is not freed until that process closes the file or restarts. df still shows the disk full, and sudo lsof +L1 lists such deleted-but-open files.
replace_subtopics.example: You SSH into a logistics customer's server where the Q&A service stopped overnight. df -h shows / at 100 percent. du -sh /var/log/* reveals a 38 GB debug log from the service. After copying the last hour off for analysis (tail -n 200000 ... > ~/debug-last-hour.log) and truncating the file with sudo truncate -s 0, the service starts again, and you add log rotation so it cannot happen twice.
replace_subtopics.code:
pwd                          # where am I?  /home/deploy
ls -lah /opt/qa-service      # long listing, hidden files, human sizes
cd /var/log                  # absolute path
cd ..                        # up one level
find /opt -name "*.env"      # find files by name
df -h                        # free disk space per filesystem
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -h  # which logs take the most space
less /etc/nginx/nginx.conf   # page through a file (q to quit, /word to search)

sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/qa/debug.log   # empty a log the service still writes to
# rm on that file would NOT free space until the service restarts:
sudo lsof +L1                # open files that were deleted (still using disk)
nano /opt/qa-service/.env.example   # Ctrl+O save, Ctrl+X exit
# vim: i to type, Esc, then :wq to save and quit, or :q! to discard

replace_subtopics.title: SSH and copying files
replace_subtopics.body:
SSH connects you to a remote machine's shell over an encrypted channel. It normally uses a key pair: a private key that stays on your laptop and a public key that is added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. ssh-keygen creates the pair. Never send the private key to anyone.

The command is ssh user@host. Often you cannot reach the server directly and must go through a jump host (also called a bastion), a single hardened machine that is the only way in; ssh -J handles that. A ~/.ssh/config file saves you from typing long options each time.

scp copies files over SSH, in either direction. rsync does the same but only sends what changed, which is better for folders. ssh -L forwards a port, so a web page running on the server's port 8000 appears on your laptop at localhost:8000 without opening it to the internet.

If your SSH connection drops, everything you started in that session is normally stopped. That is a disaster in the middle of a two-hour migration or backfill. Run long jobs inside tmux (or the older screen). tmux keeps a session alive on the server: start it with tmux new -s backfill, run the job, and detach with Ctrl+B then D. Later, even after a laptop lid closes or the VPN drops, ssh back in and run tmux attach -t backfill to see the job still running. Where tmux is not installed, nohup command > job.log 2>&1 & runs the job in the background, ignores the hang-up signal and writes its output to a file. For anything that must run every night, use a systemd service or cron instead of a terminal.
replace_subtopics.example: A bank gives you access to app-01, reachable only through bastion.bank.example. You add both to ~/.ssh/config, then 'ssh app01' takes you straight through. To check the internal admin page of the deployed service, ssh -L 8000:localhost:8000 app01 lets you open http://localhost:8000 in your own browser. Later, a 3-hour document backfill runs inside tmux on app01, so when the hotel Wi-Fi drops you reconnect and tmux attach shows it at 64 percent, still running.
replace_subtopics.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@company.com"     # create a key pair (once)

# ~/.ssh/config
# Host bastion
#     HostName bastion.bank.example
#     User jdoe
# Host app01
#     HostName 10.20.3.14
#     User deploy
#     ProxyJump bastion              # go through the jump host

ssh app01                                      # connect using the config
scp ./release.tar.gz app01:/opt/qa-service/    # copy a file up
scp app01:/var/log/qa/app.log ./               # copy a file down
rsync -avz ./config/ app01:/opt/qa-service/config/   # sync a folder
ssh -L 8000:localhost:8000 app01               # server port 8000 -> your localhost:8000

# Keep long jobs alive if SSH drops
tmux new -s backfill                           # start a named session
python backfill.py --since 2026-01-01          # run the long job inside it
# detach: Ctrl+B then D.  Reconnect later with:
tmux attach -t backfill
tmux ls                                        # list sessions

# No tmux? Run it in the background with nohup
nohup python backfill.py > backfill.log 2>&1 &
tail -f backfill.log

replace_subtopics.title: curl, jq, environment variables and cron
replace_subtopics.body:
curl sends HTTP requests from the command line, so you can test an API without writing code. -i shows response headers, -s hides the progress bar, -X picks the method, -H adds a header and -d sends a body. jq is a small tool that pretty-prints JSON and pulls out fields, for example .items[].name.

Environment variables are named values that programs read at startup, the usual place for configuration such as DATABASE_URL or an API key. export sets one in the current shell and env lists them. A service managed by systemd gets its variables from its unit file or an EnvironmentFile, not from your shell.

cron runs commands on a schedule. Each line in a crontab has five time fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) followed by the command. cron uses a minimal environment, so use absolute paths and send output to a log file.

The end of the crontab line below, >> /var/log/qa/reindex.log 2>&1, handles output. >> appends normal output (stdout) to the log file instead of overwriting it, as a single > would. 2>&1 then sends error output (stderr, stream 2) to the same place as stdout (stream 1), so tracebacks land in the log too. Without it, cron tries to email errors to a local mailbox nobody reads, and failures vanish. The terminal topic explains stdout, stderr, redirection and exit codes in full.
replace_subtopics.example: Before blaming the app, you test from the server itself: curl the local health endpoint, then curl the LLM provider's API with the key from the environment. If the local call works and the external one hangs, the customer's firewall or proxy is blocking outbound traffic, and you now have exact evidence to give their network team.
replace_subtopics.code:
curl -s http://localhost:8000/health | jq .          # local health check
curl -i https://api.example.com/v1/status            # show status line and headers

export API_TOKEN="$(cat ~/.secrets/token)"           # avoid typing secrets inline
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/ask \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"question": "What is the travel policy?"}' \
  | jq -r '.answer, .sources[].title'                # pull out fields

env | grep -i proxy                                  # any proxy settings?

# crontab -e   (min hour day month weekday command)
# 15 2 * * * /opt/qa-service/venv/bin/python /opt/qa-service/reindex.py >> /var/log/qa/reindex.log 2>&1
#   runs at 02:15 daily; >> appends stdout to the log; 2>&1 sends stderr there too

add_glossary: systemd unit file
A small config file (such as qa-service.service) that tells systemd how to run and restart a service.
Package manager
The tool that installs software from the distribution's repositories, such as apt or dnf.
logrotate
A tool that compresses and deletes old log files on a schedule.
tmux

add_subtopics.title: Streaming model answers into the page
add_subtopics.body:
A model can take ten seconds or more to write a long answer. If the page waits for the whole thing, users stare at 'Thinking...' and assume it is broken. Streaming fixes this: the server sends the answer in small pieces as the model produces them, and the page adds each piece to the screen the moment it arrives. The fastapi topic shows the server half; this subtopic is the browser half.

With fetch, the response body is a stream. res.body.getReader() gives a reader, and each await reader.read() returns the next chunk of bytes, or done: true at the end. A TextDecoder turns the bytes into text; pass { stream: true } so a character split across two chunks (an accented letter, for example) is joined correctly. Append each piece with textContent += so model output is never run as HTML.

Always add a Stop button. An AbortController gives you a signal you pass to fetch; calling controller.abort() cancels the request, the read throws an AbortError, and you can show '[stopped]'. Stopping also stops the server paying for tokens nobody will read, if the server checks for a closed connection.

Server-sent events (SSE) are a standard text format for streams: lines that start with 'data:'. The browser's EventSource object reads them for you and reconnects automatically, but it only makes GET requests with no body, so for a POST with a question you read the stream with fetch as shown and split lines yourself.

In Streamlit, st.write_stream(generator) does all of this: pass a Python generator that yields text pieces and it draws them as they come and returns the full text.

The FDE switched the backend to a streaming endpoint and the page to the reader loop below. The first words now appear in under a second, the Ask button is disabled while an answer is streaming, and a Stop button lets a partner cancel an answer that is going in the wrong direction.

add_subtopics.title: Accessibility basics for customer-facing UIs
add_subtopics.body:
Accessibility means people can use your page whatever their abilities: people who use a screen reader (software that reads the page aloud), people who only use a keyboard, and people with low vision or colour blindness. Large customers, governments and banks often require it in contracts, usually by pointing to WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) level AA. A demo that fails an accessibility check can block a pilot from going wider.

Five habits cover most problems. First, every input gets a <label> tied to it with for= and id=. Placeholder text disappears when you type and many screen readers do not read it, so it is not a label. Second, use real elements: <button> for actions and <a href> for links. A clickable <div> cannot be reached with the Tab key or pressed with Enter. Third, every meaningful image gets alt text that says what it shows; decorative images get alt="" so they are skipped. Fourth, contrast: normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background. Light grey #999999 on white is only about 2.85 to 1 and fails; #767676 is the lightest grey that passes. Never use colour alone to carry meaning, such as red for low confidence: add a word or an icon. Fifth, keep the focus outline visible (:focus-visible) so keyboard users can see where they are.

For AI pages, put aria-live="polite" on the answer area so screen readers announce new or streamed answers.

Test it: unplug the mouse and use the page with Tab, Shift+Tab and Enter only. Then run the Lighthouse accessibility audit in browser DevTools or the axe extension, and fix what they report.

A quick audit found three problems in the demo: the search box had only a placeholder, the 'Generate' control was a styled div that the keyboard could not reach, and low-confidence drafts were marked only with a pale red border. replace_subtopics.title: JavaScript basics and the DOM
replace_subtopics.body:
JavaScript declares variables with const (cannot be reassigned) and let (can be). Functions can be written with the function keyword or as arrow functions, (x) => x * 2. Objects look like Python dicts, { name: 'Ana', age: 31 }, and arrays like Python lists.

To change the page, you first find an element with document.querySelector, using the same selectors as CSS ('#answer' for an id, '.row' for a class). Then you read or set its properties, such as .value for an input or .textContent for text.

To react to the user, attach an event listener: button.addEventListener('click', handler). The browser calls your handler function whenever the event happens. Use textContent rather than innerHTML when showing text from a model or a user, because innerHTML would run any HTML inside it, which is a security risk called cross-site scripting.

A few everyday rules. Compare with === (strict equality), never ==, because == converts types first: 0 == "" is true, 0 === "" is false. JavaScript has two 'no value' markers: undefined means a variable or field was never set (a missing key in a JSON object reads as undefined), and null means someone set it to 'nothing' on purpose. Arrays have map (change every item), filter (keep matching items) and find (the first match, or undefined), which you will use on every API response. JSON.stringify turns an object into JSON text to send; JSON.parse turns JSON text back into an object. Larger code is split into modules: export a function from one file and import it in another. The typescript topic covers these language basics, promises and Node in depth.

When the page later receives a list of source documents, filter keeps only those with a score above 0.5 and map turns each one into a line of text.

replace_subtopics.title: Calling an API with fetch
replace_subtopics.body:
fetch(url, options) sends an HTTP request from the browser. It returns a Promise, an object representing a result that will arrive later. Inside an async function you write await fetch(...) to pause until the response arrives, then await res.json() to parse the body.

fetch only rejects on network failure. A 404 or 500 response still resolves, so check res.ok yourself. Show a loading state while waiting, since LLM calls can take several seconds, and show a clear message on errors.

Two rules matter for AI demos. First, never put a model provider's API key in browser code; anyone can read it in the developer tools. The browser calls your own backend, and the backend holds the key and calls the model. Second, browsers enforce CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): a page on one origin can only read responses from another origin if that server sends an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header allowing it. If your page is on localhost:5173 and your API on localhost:8000, the API must allow that origin.

When a demo breaks, open the browser DevTools first (F12, or right-click and Inspect). The Network tab lists every request the page made: click one to see the URL, method, request body, status code and the response body. A red row with status 500 means the server failed; 401 or 403 means authentication; a request marked 'CORS error' or blocked means the server did not allow your page's origin, and the Console tab will print the exact message. The Console also shows JavaScript errors with the file and line number, and anything you console.log. Most 'the button does nothing' problems are solved in these two tabs in under a minute.
replace_subtopics.example: For the HR demo, the page calls POST /ask on a small FastAPI backend with the question. The backend retrieves policy passages, calls the model with the key from its environment, and returns answer and sources. FastAPI's CORSMiddleware lists http://localhost:5173 as an allowed origin during development. When the demo first showed 'Failed to fetch', the Network tab showed the /ask request blocked, and the Console said no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header was present; adding the origin to CORSMiddleware fixed it.

replace_subtopics.title: React components at a glance
replace_subtopics.body:
React builds a page from components. A component is a function that returns JSX, an HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript. Components receive inputs called props from their parent and can keep their own data in state, created with the useState hook.

When state changes, React calls the component again and updates only the parts of the page that changed. You do not touch the DOM yourself; you change state and describe what the page should look like for that state. This makes interfaces with many moving parts much easier to keep correct.

Other hooks cover common needs: useEffect runs code after rendering, for example to load data when the component first appears. Frameworks such as Next.js add routing and server features on top of React. For a demo, a single-page app created with Vite is usually enough.

To start a project, run npm create vite@latest askbox -- --template react-ts, then npm install to download the libraries listed in package.json, then npm run dev to start a local server at http://localhost:5173 that reloads when you save. package.json is the project's manifest: it lists dependencies and scripts, short names for commands, so npm run dev, npm run build (make the files for production) and npm test run whatever the scripts section says.

An async handler must also handle failure. Wrap the request in try/catch/finally: check res.ok, store an error message in state if anything fails, and turn loading off in finally, which always runs. Without it, one failed request leaves the button disabled on 'Thinking...' for good.

Clicking a claim sets selectedId in state; React re-renders ClaimDetail with the new claim's props, with no manual DOM code. When the claims API was restarted in the middle of a demo, the fixed AskBox showed 'Server said 502' and the Ask button came back, instead of freezing.

replace_subtopics.title: A quick demo UI in Streamlit
replace_subtopics.body:
Streamlit is a Python library that turns a script into a web app. You call functions such as st.title, st.text_input, st.file_uploader and st.button, and Streamlit draws the matching widgets. Run it with 'streamlit run app.py' and it opens in the browser.

The mental model is simple: every time the user interacts with a widget, Streamlit reruns the whole script from top to bottom with the new widget values. Use st.session_state to keep values between reruns, such as a chat history, and st.cache_resource or st.cache_data to avoid reloading a model or re-reading a file on every rerun.

Because the code runs on the server in Python, API keys stay out of the browser, and you can reuse the same retrieval and model code you wrote in a notebook. The trade-off is less control over layout and behavior than React. Use Streamlit for internal demos and pilots, and move to a proper front end when the design and scale requirements grow.

For chat-style demos, st.chat_input draws a message box pinned to the bottom of the page, and st.chat_message('user') or st.chat_message('assistant') draws a chat bubble. Keep the conversation in st.session_state and redraw it on every rerun, then use st.write_stream to stream the new answer. Gradio is a similar Python library, popular for model demos, with a ready-made ChatInterface.

One safety rule: never share a demo on a public URL without authentication. A public Streamlit or Gradio link exposes the customer's documents and spends your API budget for anyone who finds it. Keep it on localhost, on the customer's network, or behind their single sign-on.
replace_subtopics.example: On day one of an engagement with a manufacturer, the FDE loads 200 maintenance manuals into a vector index in a notebook. By the afternoon the same functions sit behind a Streamlit app with an upload box, a question box and an expandable 'Sources' section, and the plant's engineers are trying it on real questions. On day two the plant asked for a chat version, so the FDE added the chat_app.py below, run only inside the plant's network.

# app.py   run with:  streamlit run app.py
import streamlit as st
from my_rag import load_index, answer_question   # your own notebook code

st.title("Maintenance manual assistant")

@st.cache_resource                       # load once, reuse across reruns
def get_index():
    return load_index("indexes/manuals")

if "history" not in st.session_state:    # survives reruns
    st.session_state.history = []

question = st.text_input("Ask about a machine or procedure")
if st.button("Ask") and question:
    with st.spinner("Searching manuals..."):
        result = answer_question(get_index(), question)   # key read from env on server
    st.session_state.history.append((question, result["answer"]))
    st.write(result["answer"])
    with st.expander("Sources"):
        for src in result["sources"]:
            st.markdown(f"- {src['title']} (page {src['page']})")


# chat_app.py   run with:  streamlit run chat_app.py
import streamlit as st
from my_rag import answer_stream        # your own code: yields text pieces

st.title("Maintenance chat")

if "messages" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.messages = []      # list of {"role": ..., "content": ...}

for m in st.session_state.messages:     # redraw the conversation on every rerun
    with st.chat_message(m["role"]):
        st.write(m["content"])

if prompt := st.chat_input("Ask about a machine"):
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": prompt})
    with st.chat_message("user"):
        st.write(prompt)
    with st.chat_message("assistant"):
        reply = st.write_stream(answer_stream(prompt, st.session_state.messages))
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

replace_subtopics.title: Methods and attributes
replace_subtopics.body:
A method is a function written inside a class. When you call o1.total(), Python quietly turns that into Order.total(o1), so self inside the method is o1. Methods read and change the object's own attributes, which keeps the logic next to the data it uses.

There are two kinds of attributes. Instance attributes live on one object (self.lines). Class attributes are defined in the class body and shared by every object, which suits constants such as a tax rate.

Python also has special methods with double underscores, often called dunder methods. __repr__ controls how the object prints, which makes debugging much easier. A leading single underscore, as in _cache, is a convention meaning 'internal, do not touch from outside'.

Three decorators change how a method is called. @property turns a method into something you read like an attribute, o1.line_count with no parentheses; use it for values computed from other attributes. @classmethod receives the class (cls) instead of an object, which makes it perfect for alternative constructors such as Order.from_row(row) that build an order from one row of a customer's CSV or JSON export. @staticmethod receives neither; it is a plain helper function that lives in the class because it belongs with it.

Two dunder methods control printing. __repr__ is for developers: it should be unambiguous and is used in the REPL, in logs and inside lists. __str__ is for people and is what print() and f-strings use; if you only write one, write __repr__, since Python falls back to it.

One trap: if you define __eq__ so that two objects compare equal by value, Python removes the default __hash__, and the objects can no longer go in a set or be dict keys. Add a matching __hash__, or use @dataclass(frozen=True), which writes both for you.
replace_subtopics.example: The distributor charges 12% VAT on every order. You store VAT_RATE once as a class attribute, add an add_line method that validates quantity, and a total method that sums the lines and applies VAT. Order 1001 with 2 bags of flour at 18.50 comes to 37.00 before VAT and 41.44 after. Harbourview Cafe's export has the id as text, a padded customer name and a price with a comma decimal, so Order.from_row and Order.parse_price clean them in one place.

replace_subtopics.title: Inheritance versus composition
replace_subtopics.body:
Inheritance lets a new class start from an existing one: class EmailNotifier(Notifier) gets all of Notifier's methods and can override some of them. Use it when the child really is a kind of the parent and can be used anywhere the parent is expected. super() calls the parent's version of a method.

Composition means a class holds other objects as attributes and asks them to do work. An OrderService has a notifier; it does not need to be one. You can pass in an email notifier in production and a fake one in tests without changing OrderService.

A good rule of thumb: prefer composition, and use inheritance for shallow 'is a' families that share one interface. Deep chains of inheritance are hard to follow because behavior is spread across many files.

A base class that only says 'children must write this method' is better written with the abc module. Inherit from ABC and mark the method with @abstractmethod. Now a child that forgets send() fails the moment you try to create it, with a clear TypeError, instead of failing later with NotImplementedError in the middle of a nightly run. typing.Protocol is a lighter option: it describes the methods an object must have, without inheritance, and a type checker such as mypy reports any object that does not match.

The same inheritance idea gives you your own exceptions. Define a small family: class IntegrationError(Exception) for anything that went wrong with a customer system, and children such as RetryableError (temporary, try again) and BadRecordError (skip this record and report it). Callers can then catch exactly the level they care about: except RetryableError to retry, except IntegrationError to catch the whole family. Always inherit from Exception, not BaseException, and give the class a docstring. The resilient topic builds retries on exactly this pattern.
replace_subtopics.example: The distributor wants confirmations by email for most cafes and by SMS for two food trucks. You write a small Notifier base class with a send method, and two children that override it. OrderService receives whichever notifier fits the customer. When a third channel (a webhook) arrives, you add one class and OrderService does not change. Later a contractor adds WebhookNotifier but forgets send(); with ABC the test suite fails immediately when the object is created. The supplier sync raises RetryableError on a 503 and BadRecordError for a row with no SKU, so the job retries the first and skips and reports the second.

replace_subtopics.title: Dataclasses and type hints
replace_subtopics.body:
Many classes are mostly records: a bundle of named fields. Writing __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ by hand for each one is tedious. The @dataclass decorator reads the annotated fields and writes those methods for you.

Type hints are the annotations after a colon, such as qty: int or lines: list[Line]. They tell readers and tools what each value should be. Python itself does not check them when the program runs; editors and a type checker such as mypy use them to catch mistakes before you run the code.

Two details matter. Mutable defaults like a list must use field(default_factory=list), or every object would share the same list. And frozen=True makes an object read-only, which is useful for values that should never change after creation, such as a parsed configuration.

Money should never be a float, because floats cannot store most decimal fractions exactly (0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004), as the dataformats topic explains. Use Decimal from the decimal module, build it from a string such as Decimal("18.50"), and round with quantize at the end.

Which record type should you pick? Use a dataclass for data your own code creates and trusts. Use a Pydantic BaseModel for data from outside, such as an API request, a customer file or an LLM's JSON output, because Pydantic checks and converts every field when the object is created and raises a clear error on bad input. Use a TypedDict when the data must stay a plain dict (for example it goes straight into json.dumps) but you still want the type checker to know its keys.
replace_subtopics.example: You rewrite Order as a dataclass with a nested Line dataclass. The file shrinks from 25 lines to 15, printing an order now shows every field, and two orders with the same data compare equal, which makes unit tests simpler. When a colleague passes qty='2' as a string, mypy flags it before it reaches the customer. After switching unit_price to Decimal, totals match the customer's invoicing system to the cent. The same order arriving through the web API is parsed with a Pydantic model instead, because that input is untrusted.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP
from typing import TypedDict

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Line:
    sku: str
    qty: int
    unit_price: Decimal          # money: Decimal, never float

@dataclass
class Order:
    order_id: int
    customer: str
    placed: date
    lines: list[Line] = field(default_factory=list)  # never lines=[]

    def total(self, vat: Decimal = Decimal("0.12")) -> Decimal:
        net = sum((l.qty * l.unit_price for l in self.lines), Decimal("0"))
        return (net * (1 + vat)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

o = Order(1001, "Lindqvist Bakery", date(2026, 3, 2))
o.lines.append(Line("flour-25kg", 2, Decimal("18.50")))  # build Decimal from a string
print(o)          # Order(order_id=1001, customer='Lindqvist Bakery', ...)
print(o.total())  # 41.44
print(0.1 + 0.2, Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))   # 0.30000000000000004 0.3

# A TypedDict only describes the shape of an ordinary dict, for the type checker
class OrderRow(TypedDict):
    order_id: int
    customer: str

row: OrderRow = {"order_id": 1001, "customer": "Lindqvist Bakery"}
print(type(row).__name__)   # dict  (still a plain dict at runtime)

replace_subtopics.title: Modules, packages and the virtual environment
replace_subtopics.body:
A module is simply a .py file. A package is a folder of modules that Python can import from, and the folder name becomes part of the import path: from orderflow.models import Order. Splitting code this way keeps each file focused on one job.

The line if __name__ == '__main__': runs only when you execute the file directly, and not when another file imports it. That lets a module be both importable and runnable.

As covered in the Python basics concepts, each project should live in its own virtual environment, a folder with its own Python and installed libraries. Pin your dependencies in requirements.txt or pyproject.toml so a colleague, or the customer's server, can rebuild exactly the same setup.

You will also see the with statement everywhere: with open(...) as f, with httpx.Client() as client, with engine.connect() as conn. An object used this way is a context manager. When the with block starts Python calls its __enter__ method, and whatever it returns goes into the name after as. When the block ends, Python calls __exit__, even if an error happened inside. That is where files get closed, connections returned and locks released, so you never leak them. You can write your own with a class that has __enter__ and __exit__, or more simply with the @contextmanager decorator from contextlib: the code before yield is the setup and the code after it, in a finally block, is the cleanup.
replace_subtopics.example: The distributor integration becomes a package called orderflow: models.py holds the dataclasses, notify.py the notifier classes, suppliers.py one adapter class per supplier file format, and cli.py the entry point the nightly job calls. Tests import from orderflow, so the same code runs in tests and in production. A db.py module in the package offers open_db(), a context manager, so every job that touches the database closes its connection even when a bad row raises an error halfway.

# Context managers, runnable as-is:
python - <<'EOF'
# ---- Context managers: what "with" does ----
import sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):                  # runs when the with block starts
        print("start")
        return self                       # this is what "as t" receives
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):  # runs when it ends, even after an error
        print("end, error:", exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else None)
        return False                      # False: do not hide the error

with Timer() as t:
    print("working")
# start / working / end, error: None

@contextmanager                           # the short way: code before yield = enter
def open_db(path):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(path)
    try:
        yield conn                        # the with block runs here
    finally:
        conn.close()                      # always closed, error or not
        print("connection closed")

try:
    with open_db(":memory:") as conn:
        conn.execute("create table t (x int)")
        raise ValueError("bad row")       # simulate a failure halfway
except ValueError as err:
    print("caught:", err)
# connection closed / caught: bad row
EOF

replace_subtopics.title: async, await and coroutines
replace_subtopics.body:
async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it does not run it; it returns a coroutine object, a paused piece of work waiting to be scheduled. You run it by awaiting it from another coroutine, by wrapping it in a task, or at the very top with asyncio.run().

await means 'pause me here until this finishes, and let other tasks run in the meantime'. You can only use await inside an async def. Anything you await must itself be awaitable, such as another coroutine, a task or asyncio.sleep.

The rule that trips beginners up: async is contagious. If a function awaits something, it must be async, and whoever calls it must await it. The chain ends at asyncio.run(main()), which you call once from ordinary code.

One place where the chain works differently is a Jupyter notebook. Jupyter already runs its own event loop, so asyncio.run(main()) in a cell fails with 'RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop'. In a notebook you simply write await main() at the top level of a cell, which Jupyter allows. When you move the code into a .py script, switch back to asyncio.run(main()).
replace_subtopics.example: You write get_parcel_status(parcel_id) as an async function. Calling get_parcel_status('PX-4411') alone prints a warning that the coroutine was never awaited and returns nothing useful. Writing status = await get_parcel_status('PX-4411') inside main, and then asyncio.run(main()), actually performs the call. When you paste the same code into a notebook to explore the carrier API, you replace the last line with await main() in its own cell.

import asyncio

async def get_parcel_status(parcel_id: str) -> dict:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.4)            # stands in for a network call
    return {"id": parcel_id, "status": "in_transit"}

async def main():
    coro = get_parcel_status("PX-4411")  # nothing has run yet
    print(type(coro))                   # <class 'coroutine'>
    status = await coro                 # now it runs, main pauses 0.4s
    print(status)

    # A task starts running as soon as the loop gets a chance
    task = asyncio.create_task(get_parcel_status("PX-4412"))
    print(await task)

asyncio.run(main())                     # the one sync-to-async bridge

# In a Jupyter notebook the loop is already running, so asyncio.run(main()) raises:
#   RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop
# Write this in a cell instead:
#   await main()

replace_subtopics.title: gather and httpx.AsyncClient for parallel API calls
replace_subtopics.body:
asyncio.gather(*coroutines) schedules every coroutine as a task and waits for all of them. The results come back as a list in the same order you passed them in, whatever order they actually finished in.

By default, the first exception raised by any task is passed to whoever awaits gather, and you lose the easy view of the other results. Passing return_exceptions=True puts exceptions into the result list instead, so you can count successes and failures.

httpx is a popular HTTP library with both sync and async clients. Create one httpx.AsyncClient and share it across all requests. It keeps a pool of open connections, which is much faster than opening a new connection per call. Always set a timeout so one stuck request cannot hang the job forever.

Python 3.11 added three helpers worth knowing. asyncio.TaskGroup is a structured alternative to gather: you create tasks inside an async with block, the block waits for all of them, and if one fails the others are cancelled and the errors are raised together, so nothing keeps running in the background by accident. asyncio.as_completed hands you results in the order they finish, which is ideal for a progress counter on a long job. asyncio.timeout(seconds) puts one deadline around a whole block, for example 'the nightly enrichment must finish in 20 minutes'.

The same pattern works for LLM calls, which is the ticket-scoring job from the WHY section. The Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs both ship async clients (AsyncAnthropic, AsyncOpenAI). Create one client, limit concurrency with a semaphore, gather one coroutine per ticket, and join the text blocks of each response. Start with 20 tickets, check the labels and the cost, then run the full set.
replace_subtopics.example: A property insurer wants 3,000 addresses geocoded through an internal API before a flood-risk analysis. You load the addresses, build one coroutine per address, and gather them through a shared AsyncClient. At the end you write 2,987 coordinates to a CSV and 13 failures (bad addresses returning 404) to a separate file for a human to fix. For a second job, a software company wants 10,000 support tickets labelled billing, bug or how-to. The same gather-plus-semaphore shape with AsyncAnthropic labels them with five calls in flight, printing progress every 500 tickets with as_completed.

import asyncio, csv
import httpx

API = "https://geo.internal.example/v1/geocode"

async def geocode(client: httpx.AsyncClient, addr: str) -> dict:
    r = await client.get(API, params={"q": addr})
    r.raise_for_status()                  # 4xx/5xx become exceptions
    return r.json()

async def main(addresses: list[str]):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:  # one shared client
        results = await asyncio.gather(
            *(geocode(client, a) for a in addresses),
            return_exceptions=True)       # keep going on failures
    ok = [(a, r) for a, r in zip(addresses, results) if not isinstance(r, Exception)]
    bad = [(a, repr(r)) for a, r in zip(addresses, results) if isinstance(r, Exception)]
    with open("failed.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
        csv.writer(f).writerows(bad)
    print(f"{len(ok)} ok, {len(bad)} failed")

# asyncio.run(main(addresses))  # add a limit before running on 3,000 rows


# ---- Modern helpers (Python 3.11+), shown with sleeps so you can run them ----
import asyncio, random

async def score(ticket_id: int) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.5))   # stands in for an API call
    return f"T{ticket_id}: ok"

async def with_taskgroup():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:           # structured: waits for all tasks
        tasks = [tg.create_task(score(i)) for i in range(5)]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]              # if one fails, the rest are cancelled

async def with_progress(n: int):
    done = 0
    for next_done in asyncio.as_completed([score(i) for i in range(n)]):
        await next_done                             # results arrive in finish order
        done += 1
        if done % 5 == 0:
            print(f"{done}/{n} done")

async def with_deadline():
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.3):            # an overall deadline for the block
            await asyncio.sleep(2)
    except TimeoutError:
        print("gave up after 0.3s")

async def main():
    print(await with_taskgroup())   # ['T0: ok', 'T1: ok', 'T2: ok', 'T3: ok', 'T4: ok']
    await with_progress(10)         # 5/10 done, then 10/10 done
    await with_deadline()           # gave up after 0.3s

asyncio.run(main())


# ---- The same pattern with an async LLM client: score support tickets ----
import asyncio, json
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5)         # stay well inside the account's rate limits

async def classify(ticket: dict) -> dict:
    async with sem:
        msg = await client.messages.create(
            model="MODEL",         # put your model id here
            max_tokens=200,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
                "Classify this support ticket as billing, bug or how-to. "
                'Reply only with JSON like {"label": "bug"}.\n\n' + ticket["text"]}],
        )
    text = "".join(b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text")
    return {"id": ticket["id"], **json.loads(text)}

async def main(tickets: list[dict]):
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(classify(t) for t in tickets), return_exceptions=True)
    ok = [r for r in results if not isinstance(r, Exception)]
    print(f"{len(ok)} labelled, {len(results) - len(ok)} failed")

replace_subtopics.title: Rate limiting with a semaphore, plus retries
replace_subtopics.body:
Gathering 3,000 requests with no limit opens thousands of connections at once. The customer's API will throttle you with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, or worse, slow down for everyone else. You need to cap your concurrency.

asyncio.Semaphore(n) is a counter with n slots. A task does async with sem: before its request. If a slot is free, it takes it and continues; if not, it waits. Leaving the block frees the slot. This limits how many requests are in flight at once.

A semaphore limits concurrency, which differs from a rate in requests per second. If the API documents a per-second limit, also space out request starts, for example with a small limiter that sleeps between starts. Retry 429 and 5xx errors with exponential backoff (waiting 1, 2, 4 seconds and so on) and respect the Retry-After header when it is present.

A careful retry helper handles three more cases. First, network failures: a timeout or a refused connection raises httpx.TimeoutException or httpx.ConnectError before there is any status code, so catch those and retry them too. Second, Retry-After can be a number of seconds ('5') or an HTTP date ('Wed, 01 Apr 2026 10:00:05 GMT'); float() on a date raises ValueError, so parse the date with email.utils.parsedate_to_datetime. Third, do not sleep after the final attempt: raise the real error at once so the caller can log it. For bigger projects the tenacity library, used in the resilient topic, gives you all of this with a decorator.
replace_subtopics.example: The geocoding API allows 20 requests per second and at most 10 concurrent connections per client. You set Semaphore(10), space starts 0.05 seconds apart, and retry up to 4 times on 429 or 5xx. The 3,000 addresses finish in about 2.5 minutes with zero throttling alerts on the customer's side. During the run, two requests hit a network timeout and one 429 came back with an HTTP-date Retry-After; all three succeeded on retry, and an address that failed four times was raised straight away into failed.csv without a pointless final wait.
checklist: Read the API docs for rate limits and concurrency limits
One shared AsyncClient with a timeout
Semaphore sized at or below the concurrency limit
Request starts spaced to the per-second limit
Retries on 429 and 5xx with backoff and jitter; honor Retry-After
Failures written to a file for a rerun
Try 50 rows first, then the full set

add_subtopics.title: Jupyter notebooks and when to leave them
add_subtopics.body:
A Jupyter notebook (.ipynb file) mixes code cells, their output (tables, charts) and notes in one document. You run cells one at a time and see results immediately, which makes notebooks excellent for the first days with customer data: loading an export, checking columns, trying a prompt on ten examples. You open them in JupyterLab in the browser or directly in VS Code.

The notebook needs a kernel, the Python process that runs the cells. Point it at the project's virtual environment, not a random global Python, by installing ipykernel into the project and registering it, as in the code below. Then imports match what your scripts use.

The big trap is hidden state. Cells can run in any order, and a variable defined in a cell you later deleted still lives in memory. A notebook can look correct and still fail for the next person. Before you share one, use Restart and Run All (or nbconvert --execute) to prove it runs top to bottom.

Outputs are saved inside the file, including rows of customer data and sometimes secrets printed by accident. Clear outputs before committing: nbstripout installs a git filter that does it automatically. Add .ipynb_checkpoints to .gitignore.

Know when to leave. As soon as a function works and will be reused, move it into src/ as a normal module with a test, and import it in the notebook. Scheduled jobs and anything the customer will run should be scripts, never notebooks. In notebooks, write await main() instead of asyncio.run (see asyncpy).

replace_subtopics.title: Virtual environments with uv or pip
replace_subtopics.body:
Every project should have its own virtual environment, a folder (by convention .venv) holding a Python interpreter link and that project's libraries. Without one, projects share the system Python and one upgrade can break another project.

pyproject.toml usually lists version ranges, such as httpx>=0.27. A lock file records the exact version of every library installed, including the libraries they depend on. Commit the lock file for applications, so every install matches what you tested; upgrade on purpose, one package at a time, and run the tests.

uv creates the environment, installs Python versions, resolves and locks dependencies, and runs commands, and it is very fast. If the customer only allows standard tools, plain venv and pip work everywhere, and pip-tools or a pip freeze file gives you a lock. Poetry is another popular all-in-one tool you may find in existing repos. The table compares them. Whichever you use, a quick check of sys.executable tells you which Python is really running, which solves many 'module not found' mysteries.

Pin the Python version too, not only the libraries. requires-python = ">=3.12" in pyproject.toml says which versions the code supports. uv python install 3.12 downloads that interpreter, and uv python pin 3.12 writes a .python-version file that uv (and tools such as pyenv) read, so everyone on the project uses the same version.

Many customers block the public package index (PyPI). They run a private index or mirror, often Artifactory or Nexus. Point pip at it with the PIP_INDEX_URL environment variable, or uv with UV_DEFAULT_INDEX or an [[tool.uv.index]] entry in pyproject.toml; ask for the URL and credentials in the first week. Some servers have no internet at all. Then build a wheelhouse, a folder of downloaded package files, on a machine that has access, copy it over, and install with --no-index --find-links so nothing is fetched from the network. Download wheels for the server's operating system, CPU and Python version, not your laptop's.
replace_subtopics.example: At Pennyrigg the nightly job fails with 'No module named pydantic' although the developer installed it. sys.executable shows the scheduler runs /usr/bin/python3, while the library went into a conda environment on his account. The fix is to run the job with uv run from the project folder, so it always uses the project's own .venv. On a later project the bank's servers had no internet. The FDE ran pip download on a Linux build box with the same Python 3.12, copied the wheelhouse folder over with the approved file transfer, and installed with --no-index. uv python pin 3.12 made sure the laptops matched the server.

replace_subtopics.title: Settings and logging configuration
replace_subtopics.body:
Settings are the values that change between environments: API URLs, tokens, batch sizes, log levels. Keep them out of the code. Read them from environment variables, check at start-up that the required ones exist, and exit with a clear message naming what is missing. Put fake examples in .env.example and keep the real .env out of git.

A small typed Settings object, a dataclass or a pydantic-settings class, gives the rest of the program one clear place to read configuration from, with types and defaults.

Configure logging once, at the program's entry point, and take the level from settings, so the customer can switch to DEBUG without editing code. Library modules only call logging.getLogger(__name__). The observability lesson shows the logging module in depth, including dictConfig and JSON output. Two rules matter most here: never log secrets such as tokens, and log the settings that matter for debugging, such as the target URL and batch size, at start-up.

For local development you keep settings in a .env file of KEY=value lines. The python-dotenv package loads it: call load_dotenv() once at start-up and the values appear in os.environ; real environment variables win over the file. pydantic-settings goes further: you declare a class with typed fields, it reads the environment and the .env file, converts types ('250' becomes the int 250), and raises a clear error listing every missing field. SecretStr hides a token when the settings are printed or logged.

Keep secrets and clutter out of git with a .gitignore at the repo root. A standard Python one lists .env, .venv/, __pycache__/, *.pyc, .ipynb_checkpoints/, .pytest_cache/, .mypy_cache/, .ruff_cache/ and dist/. Commit .env.example instead.
replace_subtopics.example: Pennyrigg's first deployment fails silently on the customer's server because CLAIMS_API_URL was never set and the code quietly defaulted to a test URL. With load_settings, the job now stops immediately with 'Missing settings: CLAIMS_API_URL', and the platform engineer fixes the deployment config in five minutes. Later the team switched to the pydantic-settings version below: a missing CLAIMS_API_TOKEN now produces a validation error naming the field, and the token prints as asterisks in the start-up log.

# src/claimsync/settings.py
import logging
import os
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    api_url: str
    api_token: str
    log_level: str = "INFO"
    batch_size: int = 500

def load_settings() -> Settings:
    missing = [k for k in ("CLAIMS_API_URL", "CLAIMS_API_TOKEN") if not os.environ.get(k)]
    if missing:                                  # fail fast and name what is missing
        raise SystemExit(f"Missing settings: {', '.join(missing)}")
    return Settings(
        api_url=os.environ["CLAIMS_API_URL"],
        api_token=os.environ["CLAIMS_API_TOKEN"],
        log_level=os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "INFO").upper(),
        batch_size=int(os.environ.get("BATCH_SIZE", "500")),
    )

def main() -> None:
    settings = load_settings()
    logging.basicConfig(level=settings.log_level,   # configured once, at the entry point
                        format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s")
    log = logging.getLogger("claimsync")
    log.info("start batch_size=%d url=%s", settings.batch_size, settings.api_url)
    # never log settings.api_token

add_subtopics.title: How sure is an eval score? Uncertainty on small AI eval sets
add_subtopics.body:
FDEs report eval results to customers all the time: 'the new prompt scores 84%', 'model B is 3 points better'. On small eval sets those numbers are much shakier than they look, and this lesson's tools tell you how shaky.

One score is a proportion: 42 correct out of 50 items. Treat it like a conversion rate and put an interval around it. The Wilson interval works well for small sets and for scores near 0% or 100%. For 42 of 50 it runs from about 71% to 92%. So '84%' really means 'somewhere between the low 70s and the low 90s'. To halve that width you need about four times as many items.

Comparing two prompts or models is different from an A/B test on users, because both versions answer the SAME items. That pairing is useful: only the items where the two disagree carry information. Count the items only B got right and the items only A got right, and test whether that split is more lopsided than a coin flip. That is McNemar's test. A paired bootstrap does the same job more generally: resample the items thousands of times, keeping A and B together for each item, and look at the spread of the difference.

In the code, prompt B scores 81% against A's 78% on 100 items. B fixes 9 items and breaks 6. McNemar's p is 0.61 and the bootstrap interval for the difference runs from -5 to +11 points, so +3 points on 100 items is very likely noise. Say so before the customer changes their production prompt. For how to build the eval set itself, see evals.
add_subtopics.example: An FDE at Harbourline Legal compared two contract-review prompts on the firm's 100-clause eval set. The new one scored 81% versus 78% and the partner wanted to switch that day. The FDE showed that the new prompt fixed 9 clauses but broke 6 others, McNemar p = 0.61, and the paired bootstrap interval crossed zero. They added 300 more labelled clauses, reran both prompts and made the call on the larger set, where the gap held at 4 points with an interval of +1 to +7.
add_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

# 1. One score: 42 of 50 eval items correct
k, n = 42, 50
low, high = proportion_confint(k, n, alpha=0.05, method="wilson")
print(f"accuracy {k/n:.0%}, 95% Wilson CI [{low:.0%}, {high:.0%}]")
# accuracy 84%, 95% Wilson CI [71%, 92%]

# 2. Two prompts on the SAME 100 items: +3 points (78% -> 81%)
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
a = np.array([1] * 78 + [0] * 22)            # prompt A: 1 = correct
b = a.copy()
b[rng.choice(np.where(a == 1)[0], 6, replace=False)] = 0   # B breaks 6 items A got right
b[rng.choice(np.where(a == 0)[0], 9, replace=False)] = 1   # B fixes 9 items A got wrong
print(a.mean(), b.mean())                    # 0.78 0.81

only_b = int(((b == 1) & (a == 0)).sum())    # items only B got right
only_a = int(((a == 1) & (b == 0)).sum())    # items only A got right
p = stats.binomtest(only_b, only_b + only_a, 0.5).pvalue   # exact McNemar test
print(f"B-only {only_b}, A-only {only_a}, McNemar p = {p:.2f}")
# B-only 9, A-only 6, McNemar p = 0.61  -> could easily be noise

# 3. Paired bootstrap: resample items, keep A and B together
diffs = []
for _ in range(10_000):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(a), len(a))
    diffs.append(b[idx].mean() - a[idx].mean())
print("95% CI for B - A:", np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5]).round(2))
# [-0.05  0.11]: includes 0, so no proven difference
checklist: Report every eval score with an interval, not a bare percentage
Use the Wilson interval for small sets or scores near 0 or 100%
Compare two systems on the same items with a paired method
Count items fixed and items broken, not just the net change
Treat a few points on about 100 items as noise until shown otherwise
Grow the eval set before making a big decision

replace_subtopics.title: Correlation versus causation
replace_subtopics.body:
Correlation measures how strongly two variables move together. Pearson's r runs from -1 (perfectly opposite) through 0 (no straight-line relationship) to +1 (perfectly together). Spearman's rho does the same on ranks and handles curved or outlier-heavy data better.

Correlation does not tell you which way the influence runs, or whether a third factor drives both. That third factor is called a confounder. Customers who use a new chatbot may spend more because they are your most engaged customers, and engagement drives both chatbot use and spending.

The cleanest way to show causation is a randomized experiment such as an A/B test. When you cannot randomize, compare before and after against a similar untouched group (difference-in-differences), control for known confounders, and be honest in the write-up about what the analysis can and cannot prove.

Simpson's paradox is a confounder in its most surprising form: a rate that looks better overall can be worse inside every single group. It happens when the groups are mixed in different proportions. In the code below the new triage tool resolves 76% of tickets overall against 58% for the old one, yet it is worse at both sites. The new tool was mostly used at Leeds, where tickets are easy, and the old one mostly at Porto, where they are hard. Whenever you compare rates, split them by the obvious segments (site, channel, customer size) before you conclude anything.

Two biases come from which data you get to see. Survivorship bias means looking only at the cases that made it through: studying only customers who renewed tells you nothing about why others left. Selection bias means the people in your data chose, or were chosen, in a way linked to the outcome: pilot users who volunteered for a new AI tool are usually the keenest staff, so their results overstate what everyone else will get.
replace_subtopics.example: A bank sees that branches with more ATMs have more fraud. Removing ATMs would not reduce fraud: busy city branches have both more ATMs and more transactions, and more transactions produce more fraud cases. When you divide fraud cases by transactions, the correlation with ATM count almost disappears. In a second case, a support team reported that its new AI triage tool resolved 76% of tickets against 58% for the old one. Split by site, the new tool was worse in both Leeds and Porto; it simply handled far more of the easy Leeds tickets.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

traffic = rng.uniform(1_000, 20_000, size=200)        # confounder
atms = np.round(traffic / 4_000 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 200))
fraud = 0.002 * traffic + rng.normal(0, 4, 200)       # driven by traffic only

r, p = stats.pearsonr(atms, fraud)
print(f"ATMs vs fraud: r = {r:.2f}")                  # strong, but misleading

rate = fraud / traffic * 10_000                       # fraud per 10k transactions
r2, _ = stats.pearsonr(atms, rate)
print(f"ATMs vs fraud rate: r = {r2:.2f}")            # much weaker
rho, _ = stats.spearmanr(atms, fraud)
print(f"Spearman rho = {rho:.2f}")


import pandas as pd

# Simpson's paradox: resolution rate of an AI triage tool at two sites
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "site":     ["Leeds", "Leeds", "Porto", "Porto"],
    "tool":     ["old",   "new",   "old",   "new"],
    "tickets":  [100,     400,     400,     100],

})

# {'new': 0.76, 'old': 0.58}   pooled: new looks far better

# site
# Leeds  0.85  0.9
# Porto  0.40  0.5     inside each site the new tool is WORSE
