replace_subtopics.title: A/B tests and statistical significance
replace_subtopics.body:
In an A/B test, each user is randomly assigned to A or B. Random assignment is the key idea: it makes the two groups alike in every way except the change you made, so a difference in results can be credited to that change.

The null hypothesis says the change has no effect. The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least as large as yours if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value, conventionally below 0.05, means your result would be unusual under 'no effect', so you call it statistically significant. The 0.05 cut-off is a convention, so treat it as a guide.

Always report three things together: the observed difference, its confidence interval and the p-value. For conversion rates, a two-proportion z-test or a chi-square test is standard. For averages such as order value, use Welch's t-test, which does not assume both groups have equal variance.

Many business metrics are heavily skewed: basket size, handle time, claim value. A few huge values make averages jumpy, and the t-test's assumptions get shaky with small samples. Two safer options: a bootstrap confidence interval of the difference (resample each group, compute B minus A, repeat thousands of times, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles), or the Mann-Whitney U test, which compares the two whole distributions using ranks and does not need normal data. Mann-Whitney answers 'does B tend to produce larger values?', not 'is the mean larger?', so say which question you answered.

Ratio metrics such as revenue per visitor or tickets per agent need care too. The unit you randomized (the user) is not always the unit in the ratio (sessions, orders), and one user's many sessions are not independent. Compute the metric per randomized user first, or use a bootstrap that resamples whole users.
replace_subtopics.example: A grocery delivery app tests a new checkout page. Control: 520 orders from 10,000 visitors (5.20%). Variant: 585 from 10,000 (5.85%). The lift is 0.65 points, p is about 0.044, and the 95% interval runs from roughly 0.02 to 1.28 points. The effect is probably real, but it might be tiny. Then you check average basket size with Welch's t-test to make sure the new page did not trade conversions for smaller orders. Because basket sizes are skewed, you confirm the basket result with a bootstrap interval and a Mann-Whitney test: both agree there is no clear difference.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Conversion: chi-square test on a 2x2 table [converted, not converted]
table = np.array([[520, 10_000 - 520],
                  [585, 10_000 - 585]])
chi2, p_conv, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table, correction=False)
print(f"conversion p = {p_conv:.3f}")   # about 0.044, same as the z-test

# Basket size: Welch's t-test (unequal variances)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
basket_a = rng.gamma(4, 12.0, size=520)     # euros per order, group A
basket_b = rng.gamma(4, 11.8, size=585)     # group B
t, p_basket = stats.ttest_ind(basket_b, basket_a, equal_var=False)
print(f"basket A {basket_a.mean():.2f}, B {basket_b.mean():.2f}, p = {p_basket:.2f}")

# Skewed metrics (basket size): bootstrap CI of the difference, and Mann-Whitney U
diffs = [rng.choice(basket_b, len(basket_b)).mean() - rng.choice(basket_a, len(basket_a)).mean()
         for _ in range(5_000)]
print("B - A basket, 95% CI:", np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5]).round(2))
u, p_mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(basket_b, basket_a)   # compares whole distributions, no normality needed
print(f"Mann-Whitney p = {p_mw:.2f}")
# B - A basket, 95% CI: [-3.57  2.01]  -> includes 0
# Mann-Whitney p = 0.76
checklist: Hypothesis and one primary metric written down before launch
Users (not page views) randomly assigned, and they stay in their group
Sample size and run length fixed in advance, covering full weeks
Group sizes checked for the expected split (sample ratio check)
Guardrail metrics watched, such as refunds or page errors
Result reported as lift, 95% CI and p-value
Decision recorded, including inconclusive results

replace_subtopics.title: Sample size, power and peeking
replace_subtopics.body:
Before a test starts, decide how many users you need. The inputs are the baseline rate, the minimum detectable effect (MDE, the smallest lift worth acting on), the significance level (usually 0.05) and the power, the chance of detecting the effect if it really exists (usually 0.8). Small effects on small rates need large samples.

Peeking means checking the p-value repeatedly and stopping as soon as it dips below 0.05. Because the p-value wanders up and down by chance, checking daily gives many chances to cross the line, and the real false positive rate can climb well above 5%. Fix the sample size and look once, or use a method designed for continuous monitoring, such as a sequential test.

Testing many metrics or many segments has the same problem. With 20 independent comparisons at 0.05, you expect about one false win by chance alone. Name one primary metric in advance and treat the rest as exploratory, or correct for multiple comparisons.

Before reading any result, check that the split itself worked. If you planned 50/50 but got 50,600 users in A and 49,100 in B, that is a sample ratio mismatch (SRM). A chi-square test against the planned split tells you whether the gap is bigger than chance. SRM almost always means a bug: a redirect that drops some users, a bot filter applied to one group, or a crash in one app version. The result cannot be trusted until you find the cause. Check SRM for each major segment too, because the bug often hits only one browser, device or country.
replace_subtopics.example: A subscription meal-kit company converts 4% of trial users to paid. They want to detect an increase to 4.4% (a 10% relative lift). The formula below says they need roughly 39,500 trial users per group. With 6,000 new trials a week split in two, the test must run about 13 weeks, so you suggest testing a bolder change with a larger expected effect instead. When the test finally ran, group A had 50,600 users and group B 49,100. The SRM check gave p = 0.000002, and splitting by platform showed Android users were missing from B because of a crash in the new flow. The team fixed the crash and restarted the test.
replace_subtopics.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

def sample_size_per_group(p1, p2, alpha=0.05, power=0.8):
    """Users per group for a two-sided test of two proportions."""
    z_a = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2)     # 1.96 for alpha 0.05
    z_b = stats.norm.ppf(power)             # 0.84 for power 0.8
    p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2
    num = (z_a * np.sqrt(2 * p_bar * (1 - p_bar))
           + z_b * np.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2))) ** 2
    return int(np.ceil(num / (p2 - p1) ** 2))

n = sample_size_per_group(0.04, 0.044)
print(n)                                  # about 39,500 per group
print(f"weeks at 3,000 per group per week: {n / 3_000:.1f}")
print(sample_size_per_group(0.04, 0.05))  # a bigger lift needs far fewer

# Sample ratio mismatch (SRM): did the 50/50 split really happen?
counts = [50_600, 49_100]                    # users actually in A and B
chi2, p_srm = stats.chisquare(counts)        # expected: equal split
print(f"A share {counts[0] / sum(counts):.1%}, SRM p = {p_srm:.6f}")
# A share 50.8%, SRM p = 0.000002  -> the split is broken, do not trust the result

# Check each segment too: a bug often hits one browser or app version
for seg, a, b in [("web", 30_100, 29_900), ("ios", 12_000, 12_050), ("android", 8_500, 7_150)]:
    print(seg, round(stats.chisquare([a, b]).pvalue, 4))
# web 0.4142
# ios 0.7471
# android 0.0      <- android users are missing from B

add_glossary: Wilson interval
A confidence interval for a proportion that behaves well for small samples and rates near 0 or 100%.
Paired comparison
Comparing two systems on the same items, so only the items where they disagree carry information.
McNemar's test
A test for paired yes-or-no results that checks whether items fixed and items broken are more lopsided than chance.
Paired bootstrap
Resampling items with replacement while keeping both systems' results for each item together, to get an interval for their difference.
Simpson's paradox
A pattern where a comparison overall reverses inside every subgroup because the groups are mixed in different proportions.
Survivorship bias
Drawing conclusions only from cases that made it through a filter, ignoring those that dropped out.
Selection bias
Distortion caused when the people or items in the data were chosen in a way linked to the outcome.
Mann-Whitney U test
A rank-based test of whether one group tends to have larger values than another, without assuming normal data.
Sample ratio mismatch
When the actual split between test groups differs from the planned split by more than chance, usually a sign of a bug.

add_subtopics.title: Palantir today: AIP bootcamps and the titles to search for
add_subtopics.body:
The Echo and Delta story is Palantir's early history. Interviewers today often refer to its newer motion too, so know it.

In 2023 Palantir launched AIP, its Artificial Intelligence Platform. AIP lets customers put large language models to work on top of their own data and workflows in Foundry and Gotham, with controls on what the model can see and do. To sell it, Palantir ran AIP bootcamps: short, hands-on sessions, often one to five days, where the customer's own people sit with Palantir engineers and build working use cases on their real data. The customer leaves with something running instead of a slide deck, and the best use cases turn into paid deployments.

This is the FDE model compressed. The old version spent weeks on site before showing value; the bootcamp shows value in days, then the forward team stays to take it to production. Many AI companies copy the idea with pilot sprints and hackathons at the customer.

When you look for these jobs, one title will not find them all. Search for each variant: Forward Deployed Engineer, Forward Deployed AI Engineer, Forward Deployed Software Engineer, Applied AI Engineer, AI Deployment Engineer and Deployment Strategist (the Echo side). At some AI labs, roles called Solutions Engineer or Solutions Architect are also hands-on builders. Read the verbs in the posting: 'build, ship, deploy' points to FDE work. The fderoles topic explains how each title differs by company type.

replace_subtopics.title: How FDEs differ from similar roles
replace_subtopics.body:
Several customer-facing technical roles sound alike. The short version: the difference comes down to who writes production code, and when they are involved.

A Sales Engineer (also called a pre-sales Solutions Engineer) runs demos and small proofs before the sale, and does not ship production code. A Solutions Architect (SA) designs and advises, mostly before the sale. An Implementation or Professional Services engineer configures the product to match a statement of work (SOW) and rarely feeds the product roadmap. A Customer Success Engineer (CSE) helps customers adopt the product after the sale. A technology consultant bills hours and hands over documents or custom code that does not feed a product.

An FDE writes and ships production code inside the customer, on the vendor's platform, and feeds lessons back into the product. A commonly quoted, rough estimate is that FDEs spend 70 to 80 percent of their time on code and model work; it varies a lot by company and seniority.

This is only a summary. The fderoles topic compares these roles in depth: where each sits in the deal, a week in the life of an FDE, and how to move between them.
replace_subtopics.example: A bank buys an AI document-processing product. The Sales Engineer ran the demo on sample loan forms. The SA drew the architecture diagram during the sales cycle. The FDE builds the connector to the bank's loan system and tunes extraction for 12 loan forms. An implementation engineer later sets up user roles and templates in a second business unit, following the SOW. Six months later the CSE runs quarterly reviews and training.

add_subtopics.title: Paying for FDE time: services models
add_subtopics.body:
Somebody has to pay for the FDE hours. How the vendor charges for them changes the company's reported numbers, so leadership argues about it often.

Option one: bundle the FDE effort into the platform price. The customer sees one subscription. All FDE cost lands in COGS with no matching services revenue, so gross margin drops the most, but every dollar counts as recurring ARR and later NRR.

Option two: bill the FDE work as professional services under a statement of work (SOW). A fixed fee means one price for a defined scope; if the work runs over, the vendor absorbs it. Time and materials (T&M) means the customer pays per hour, so overruns are billed. Services revenue is not recurring, so investors value it far less than ARR, and services margin is often near zero or even negative, because vendors price it low to win the software deal.

A common middle path is a paid pilot: the customer pays a modest fee for the first weeks, and that fee is credited against year one if they sign. Paying anything filters out customers who are only curious.

Leaders also watch the services attach rate: the share of deals that include a paid SOW. A high rate can mean the product is hard to use without help.

The code shows one deal three ways. The psa topic covers how services teams run these contracts day to day, and the roi topic covers how the customer's own pricing (seats, usage, outcomes) works.
add_subtopics.example: Tallowby, an AI claims vendor, sold a $600k platform deal needing 1,200 FDE hours. Bundled, the account's gross margin was 55 percent. As a $120k fixed-fee SOW it rose to 62 percent overall, with services margin at minus 25 percent. Billed as T&M at $175 per hour, it reached 67 percent. The CFO chose T&M for integration-heavy accounts, plus an $80k paid pilot credited against year one for new customers.

# One $600k-a-year platform deal plus 1,200 hours of FDE work

    cogs = SOFTWARE_COGS + fde_cost
    total = (revenue - cogs) / revenue
    svc = (services_revenue - fde_cost) / services_revenue if services_revenue else None
    svc_txt = f"{svc:.0%}" if svc is not None else "n/a"
    print(f"{name:<26} revenue {revenue:>9,}  gross margin {total:.0%}  services margin {svc_txt}")

show("Fixed-fee SOW $120k", 120_000)

replace_subtopics.title: Unit economics and gross margin
replace_subtopics.body:
Revenue is the money customers pay. Cost of goods sold (COGS) is what it costs to deliver the product: cloud hosting, support, and for FDE companies, a share of engineer salaries. Gross margin is (revenue minus COGS) divided by revenue.

Pure software companies often have high gross margins because serving one more user costs very little. Putting engineers on customer projects raises COGS, so the margin drops.

This lower margin is the 'margin' side of the margin-for-moat trade. It is a real cost and you should not hide it. The question is what the company gets in return.

AI companies carry one more cost that classic SaaS does not: model inference. Every request to a language model costs money, whether the vendor pays an API provider or runs its own GPUs, and that cost sits in COGS. So AI companies often start with gross margins below the classic SaaS level, which is often quoted at around 75 to 80 percent, before a single FDE is added. The margin-for-moat trade stacks on top of that lower starting point, which is why FDE teams at AI companies are pushed hard to turn repeated work into product.
replace_subtopics.example: A company earns $10M in annual revenue. Hosting and support cost $1.5M. With no FDEs, gross margin is 85 percent. It then assigns 8 FDEs at a loaded cost of $250k each to customer work, adding $2M to COGS. Gross margin falls to 65 percent. If the same company is an AI vendor paying $1.2M a year for model inference, it starts at 73 percent before FDEs and falls to 53 percent with them.

revenue = 10_000_000
hosting_support = 1_500_000
fde_count, fde_cost = 8, 250_000          # loaded cost per FDE per year

def gross_margin(rev, cogs):
    return (rev - cogs) / rev

print("no FDEs:  ", round(gross_margin(revenue, hosting_support), 2))   # 0.85
cogs_fde = hosting_support + fde_count * fde_cost
print("with FDEs:", round(gross_margin(revenue, cogs_fde), 2))          # 0.65

# An AI company also pays for model inference on every request

cogs_ai = hosting_support + inference
print("AI, no FDEs:  ", round(gross_margin(revenue, cogs_ai), 2))                         # 0.73
print("AI with FDEs: ", round(gross_margin(revenue, cogs_ai + fde_count * fde_cost), 2))  # 0.53

replace_subtopics.title: Net Revenue Retention explained
replace_subtopics.body:
Net Revenue Retention (NRR) measures how revenue from a fixed group of existing customers changes over a period, usually a year. ARR means annual recurring revenue.

The formula is (starting ARR + expansion - contraction - churn) divided by starting ARR. Expansion is extra spending from upsells or new teams. Contraction is customers reducing spend. Churn is customers leaving.

NRR above 100 percent means the existing customer base grows even if you sign no new customers. FDE-heavy companies aim to push this number up, because deep deployments tend to expand into more teams and use cases.

At AI vendors that charge by usage (tokens, documents, calls), expansion often arrives as consumption growth rather than a new contract. A team that starts sending twice as many documents doubles its spend without anyone signing anything. This makes NRR volatile: a busy quarter lifts it, a quiet month or a switch to a cheaper model lowers it. Leaders often look at a trailing average or at committed spend to smooth it out.

Keep two kinds of churn apart. Logo churn counts customers lost, as a share of all customers. Revenue churn counts ARR lost, as a share of starting ARR. Losing two tiny customers out of four is 50 percent logo churn but may be only 5 percent revenue churn. Report both.
replace_subtopics.example: A company starts the year with $20M ARR from 40 customers. During the year, those customers add $6M through expansion, two customers cut $1M, and three customers worth $1.5M leave. NRR = (20 + 6 - 1 - 1.5) / 20 = 117.5 percent. A usage-priced account that spent $100k in January and $205k in December grew its run-rate from $1.2M to $2.46M with no new contract. Separately, a cohort that loses two of four customers can show 50 percent logo churn but only 5 percent revenue churn if the lost customers were small.
replace_subtopics.code:
def nrr(start_arr, expansion, contraction, churn):
    """Net Revenue Retention for one cohort over one period."""
    return (start_arr + expansion - contraction - churn) / start_arr

# Cohort: customers active on 1 Jan, measured on 31 Dec
print(f"{nrr(20.0, 6.0, 1.0, 1.5):.1%}")   # 117.5%

# Gross Revenue Retention ignores expansion: shows pure leakage
grr = (20.0 - 1.0 - 1.5) / 20.0
print(f"GRR {grr:.1%}")                     # 87.5%

# Usage-priced AI vendor: expansion arrives as consumption, month by month
monthly_spend = [100, 104, 112, 131, 118, 140, 165, 150, 172, 190, 176, 205]  # $k, one account
print("run-rate ARR Jan:", monthly_spend[0] * 12, " Dec:", monthly_spend[-1] * 12)

replace_subtopics.title: When SLG works and when it fails
replace_subtopics.body:
SLG works when field work turns into product. Over time, the same deployment should need fewer FDE hours, and gross margin should rise as a result.

SLG fails when every deployment stays bespoke. Then margins never improve, and the company behaves like a consulting firm with a software licence attached.

A simple health check is to track FDE hours per new deployment over time, alongside NRR. You want the first number going down and the second staying high.

Leadership also judges FDE-heavy accounts with two companion metrics. CAC payback is how many months of gross profit from a customer it takes to repay the customer acquisition cost (CAC): the sales, pre-sales and early FDE spending needed to win the account. Many companies aim for well under 24 months. LTV:CAC compares the lifetime value of a customer (yearly gross profit divided by the yearly churn rate, in the simple version) with CAC; a ratio of about 3 or more is a commonly quoted healthy target. Heavy FDE work lowers the account's margin, which lengthens payback, so it has to be earned back through expansion and low churn.
replace_subtopics.example: Company A's first 5 deployments took 3,000 FDE hours each. By deployments 16 to 20, the average was 1,100 hours because connectors and templates were productised. Company B's average stayed at 2,900 hours. Company A is running SLG well. Company B is at risk of becoming a consultancy. For one account, Company A spent $400k to win a $600k deal at 55 percent gross margin: payback is about 14.5 months and LTV:CAC about 8, so the FDE investment pays back.

def trend(hours):

print("A:", trend(company_a))   # -0.54

add_glossary: Statement of work (SOW)
A contract that defines the scope, deliverables, schedule and price of services work.
Fixed fee
A services price agreed in advance for a defined scope; the vendor absorbs overruns.
Time and materials (T&M)
A services price based on hours actually worked at an agreed rate; the customer pays for overruns.
Paid pilot
A short, paid trial whose fee is often credited against the first year if the customer signs.
Services attach rate
The share of deals that include a paid services contract.
Inference cost
The cost of running a model on each request, counted in COGS at AI companies.
Logo churn
The share of customers lost in a period, counted by customer rather than by revenue.
Revenue churn
The share of starting ARR lost to cancellations in a period.
CAC payback
Months of gross profit from a customer needed to repay the cost of acquiring it.
LTV:CAC
A customer's lifetime gross profit divided by the cost of acquiring it.
